title: Visual Target - Creative Director Notes
summary: What makes the visual target work and how Bobby implements it. The gap analysis between current dashboard and the north star.
content:
Visual Target: Creative Director Notes

Steffen | 2026-03-16 For Bobby. This is what you're building toward.

The Three Variations

  1. full-office-warm-night.png -- Late night. Office glows like a jewel box against the void. Best for: the default dashboard state. Warm, alive, inviting.
  2. full-office-golden-hour.png -- Late afternoon. Directional sunlight from the west. Best for: showing lighting quality and depth. The most "real" feeling.
  3. full-office-game-ui.png -- Game world with UI elements. Logo, minimap, nameplates, status indicators. Best for: showing the FULL PRODUCT vision including UI chrome.

Recommendation: V1 (warm night) is the primary target for the default game view. V3 (game UI) shows where the UI elements go. V2 (golden hour) is a stretch goal for time-of-day lighting shifts.

THE GAP: Current Dashboard vs. Visual Target

What the current dashboard does WRONG:

  • Flat image rotation. Room concept PNGs are placed on a CSS-transformed plane. They look like playing cards scattered on a table, not rooms in a building.
  • No shared walls. Each room is an isolated island. No visual connection between rooms.
  • No depth. No shadows, no light spill, no 3D wall thickness. Everything exists on a single z-plane.
  • No ground plane. Rooms float in a void with no anchor point. No sense of "this is a place."
  • No atmosphere. No fog, no light bloom, no ambient particles. The void is just empty black.
  • Labels on top of images. Agent names sit on the images rather than being part of the world (nameplates, room signs).

What the visual target does RIGHT:

  • Connected architecture. Rooms share walls. When you see Bobby's room you also see Colton's and Steffen's walls. It reads as one building.
  • Light as depth cue. Warm light pools from desk lamps create depth. Monitor glow reflects on walls. Window light spills onto floors.
  • 3D wall thickness. Walls have visible depth. You can see the cut edge. This is cutaway architecture, not a flat grid.
  • Distinct room personalities. Bobby's purple vs. Elon's green vs. Steffen's golden sun. Each room's light signature is different.
  • Characters as life. Small figures at desks make the office feel alive. It's not a building. It's a workplace.
  • The CORNER sign. It's a lit sign on the building facade, not a logo overlay. It's part of the world.
  • Ground plane context. The building sits ON something, with light spilling down onto it. It has physical presence.

Implementation Notes for Bobby

Priority 1: Shared Walls (kills the "card scatter" effect)

  • Stop rendering rooms as isolated images on a transformed plane
  • Build a unified isometric grid where rooms are CELLS in a connected structure
  • Shared walls render once between adjacent rooms, not twice
  • Wall thickness: exterior 4px, interior 2px (at the grid scale)
  • CSS custom properties or SVG for wall rendering, not rotated PNGs

Priority 2: Lighting System (creates depth without 3D)

  • Each room has a base ambient color (warm amber for most, cool blue-green for Elon)
  • CSS radial-gradient overlays simulate desk lamp pools of light
  • Monitor glow: colored box-shadow or radial gradient from monitor positions
  • Window light: linear-gradient from window positions, warm gold (#FFD87A)
  • Bobby's purple LED: a purple radial gradient along desk edges
  • These all layer with mix-blend-mode to create rich lighting

Priority 3: Ground Plane and Atmosphere

  • The building sits on a subtle ground plane (1-2 shade lighter than the void)
  • Light spill from windows extends PAST the building exterior onto this ground
  • Subtle CSS gradient fog at building base (4-6px, very transparent)
  • Optional: faint particle animation in the void (tiny dots drifting, very subtle)

Priority 4: Characters

  • Use the sprite assets from generate-c2-assets.py (Steffen generates, Bobby places)
  • Each agent's idle sprite sits at their desk position within the room
  • Characters are small but visible. They're the life indicator.
  • Active agents have a subtle glow pulse around their sprite

Priority 5: The CORNER Sign

  • Render as part of the building's south facade
  • Warm backlit glow (text-shadow or box-shadow in amber)
  • Not a floating UI element. It's architecture.

Priority 6: Game UI Elements (from V3)

  • Minimap: bottom-left, showing L-shaped layout as colored squares
  • Status dots: green/amber/red per room (from agent status API)
  • Room nameplates: pixel font, positioned above each room in the isometric grid
  • CORNER logo: top-left, using the standard brand mark

Depth Techniques That Make This Work

  1. Occlusion. Front rooms partially overlap/block back rooms. This is the #1 depth cue. The isometric grid handles this automatically if rooms are rendered back-to-front (painter's algorithm).

  2. Atmospheric perspective. Rooms further from camera are VERY slightly lighter/hazier. 2-3% opacity difference. Barely perceptible but it adds depth.

  3. Light direction consistency. All warm light sources come from the upper-left (NW). All shadows fall to the lower-right (SE). Every element follows this. No exceptions.

  4. Color temperature separation. Warm interior (amber, gold) vs. cool exterior (navy, dark blue). The contrast between inside and outside is what makes it feel cozy and inviting.

  5. Edge lighting. The roof line of the building catches just a hint of warm light on its upper edge. CSS border-top with a subtle warm color. This separates the building from the void.

  6. Layered rendering. Floor > furniture > characters > walls > roof edge > light overlays > fog. Each layer adds depth. Skip a layer and it flattens.

Color Reference

Element Hex Usage
Void #0A0F1E Background, everything outside the building
Ground plane #111827 Subtle surface under the building
Exterior wall #4A5568 Building shell, slightly warm gray
Interior wall #718096 Room dividers, lighter and thinner
Wood floor (warm) #C4956A Steffen, Main Hall, Patrik
Wood floor (dark) #5A4A3A Bobby, Cleo
Tile floor #8B9DAF Elon, Elmo
Window glow #FFD87A All windows, primary warmth source
Bobby LED #9C27B0 Purple underglow, Bobby's signature
Elon glow #4CAF50 Green terminal/server light
Monitor blue #4FC3F7 Default monitor glow
Ambient warm #FFB74D Desk lamps, pendant lights
CORNER sign #FFD87A with #FFB74D glow Building nameplate

The Standard

Compare every iteration against these visual target images. When the live dashboard feels like you're looking at a living office from above in a premium indie game, we've arrived. Until then, keep pushing.

The individual room concepts (bobby-room-concept.png, elon-room-concept.png, etc.) show the QUALITY bar for each room. These full-office targets show the COMPOSITION bar for the whole building. Both must be met.

This is the north star. Every commit gets us closer to this image.
